lessons.title: Correlation is not a cause

steps.headline: A correlation coefficient, r, gives a relationship's direction by its sign and its strength by its size.

lead.text: r runs from −1 to +1. A plus sign means both measures rise together. A minus sign means one rises as the other falls. The further r is from zero, either way, the tighter the points follow a line.
The sign tells you which way, and the size tells you how tightly. Neither tells you why.

steps.headline: Squaring r gives the share of variation that two measures have in common.

lead.text: People differ on both measures. Square r to see how much of that difference is shared. For r = 0.4, the square is 0.16, so 16% of the differences are shared.
Squaring removes the sign. A negative r shares variation just as a positive one does.
In the first case, people who slept more had faster reaction times: the points slope downhill, so r is negative. The correlation here is r = −0.6.

reveal.text: You squared r. A negative number squared is positive, so the sign drops out. The other 64% of the differences in reaction time are unrelated to sleep in this sample.

steps.headline: A third variable that drives both measures can create a correlation that neither one causes.

lead.text: On hot days, more people buy ice cream and more people swim. Neither causes the other. A hidden variable that drives both is called a confound.
You see the pattern but not the confound. That is why a correlation alone cannot show a cause.

steps.headline: Do ice-cream sales still track pool rescues when temperature is held roughly fixed?

workedSteps.text: Look at every day of the year. Sales and rescues rise together.
Colour the days by temperature. The high-sales days are the hot days, and so are the high-rescue days.
Keep only days at 21–23 °C. Within them, higher sales no longer go with more rescues.
So temperature, not ice cream, was moving both measures.

lead.text: Swapping the axes leaves r exactly the same. A correlation is symmetric, so the data alone cannot say which way an arrow points.

reveal.text: Running the arrow from mood to exercise is called reverse causation. Only a design that controls who exercises, such as an experiment, can separate the two directions.

lead.text: Staff remember the chaotic full-moon shifts and forget the quiet ones. To test the belief, count every shift, not just the vivid ones.

reveal.text: Both groups were busy at the same rate, so the full moon changes nothing. Believing in a relationship the counts do not show is an illusory correlation. Compare rates in every cell rather than recalling vivid cases.

model.setting: Emergency-department shifts under a full moon

lessons.orientation: Read the sign and strength of a correlation, then look for what else could produce it.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In one seaside town, ice-cream sales and pool rescues rise and fall together through the year. The busiest ice-cream weeks are also the busiest weeks for rescues.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a correlation's direction, strength and shared variation, and name three ways two things move together without a cause.

recap.keyIdea: A correlation gives direction, strength and shared variation, but never the cause. A confound, a reversed arrow or a vivid memory can each produce a pattern that no cause explains.

blocks.text: You squared r = −0.6 to find that two measures share 36% of their variation. You saw the ice-cream link vanish once temperature was held steady, and found that 6 of 20 and 30 of 100 are the same busy rate.

recap.nextHook: Correlation cannot separate these explanations. Random assignment can, by building the comparison yourself.

lessons.title: Random assignment

steps.headline: Random assignment gives every participant an equal chance of landing in either group.

lead.text: When people pick their own group, the keenest often pick the programme and bring a head start with them. This is self-selection. A random draw, such as a coin toss, ignores who they are.
Random assignment decides by the draw, never by the person.
Eight people can choose. Four volunteers who exercise 9, 8, 8 and 7 hours a week choose the new programme. The other four exercise 3, 2, 2 and 1 hours a week.

reveal.text: That is a head start before anything is done. Any later difference in fitness could be this gap, not the programme. You just saw self-selection build a confound into the design.

steps.headline: Compare the average fitness of two groups made by a random draw.

workedSteps.text: Group A had prior fitness scores 5, 9, 4 and 6. Add them and divide by 4.
Group B had scores 7, 3, 8 and 10. Do the same.
Subtract A from B. Nothing has been done to either group yet, so this gap is chance.
Draw again and the gap changes. The draw never favours either group in the long run.

steps.headline: Name what you set and what you measure, and say exactly how you will measure it.

lead.text: Say a study gives people caffeine or none, then times their reactions. The variable the experimenter sets is the independent variable. The one measured to show its effect is the dependent variable. An operational definition says exactly how to measure a concept.
Naming all of this before the data arrive stops you hunting for an outcome that happens to differ.
Researchers assign people at random to a fitness programme or no programme. After three months they measure each person's resting heart rate.

reveal.text: Resting heart rate is measured afterwards to see the programme's effect, so it is the dependent variable. Whether a person does the programme is the independent variable.

steps.headline: A placebo and blinding keep expectation equal, so only the treatment differs.

lead.text: People improve partly because they expect to. A placebo group takes an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient. In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the people measuring them know who received what.
The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time produce alone.
A drug trial gives one group the drug and another an identical-looking placebo. Both groups improve on a symptom score.

reveal.text: The placebo group's improvement is what expectation and time produce without the active ingredient. Only the difference between the groups can be credited to the drug.

lessons.orientation: See why only random assignment to conditions lets an experiment rule out confounds.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A gym lets members choose whether to join its new fitness programme. Three months later, the joiners are fitter than the members who stayed out. A friend says: “That proves the programme works.”

intro.promise: By the end you'll say why random assignment rules out confounds, and name the variables, placebo and blinding a fair trial needs.

recap.keyIdea: Random assignment gives everyone an equal chance of each condition, so no trait systematically favours one group. Placebos and blinding then keep expectation equal, and the gap that remains is the treatment.

blocks.text: You found that volunteers who chose the programme started 6 hours a week ahead, and that a chance gap of 0.5 is not a bias. You also found that a drug's own effect is 12 − 8 = 4 points once the placebo response is removed.

recap.nextHook: Is a difference big enough to matter, and will it appear again if someone repeats the study?

lessons.title: How big, and will it replicate?

steps.headline: Cohen's d measures a difference between two means in units of standard deviation.

lead.text: A gain means little until you know the spread of scores. Divide the difference between the means by the standard deviation, and you get d. A gain of 10 points when scores spread by 20 gives d = 0.5.
Cohen's rough labels are 0.2 small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large. He warned they are no substitute for knowing the field.
A control group has a mean score of 100. A training group has a mean of 106. The standard deviation is 15 in both groups.

reveal.text: You divided a 6-point difference by a spread of 15. Doubling the gain to 12 points would give d = 0.8, and the two curves would visibly separate.

steps.headline: Find d for groups with means 30 and 38 and standard deviations 2 and 14.

workedSteps.text: The standard deviations differ, so pool them. Square each one.
Average the squares, then take the square root. This is the pooled SD.
Divide the difference between the means by the pooled SD.

steps.headline: Statistical power is the chance a study detects an effect that is really there.

lead.text: A rule of thumb from Lehr says a study needs about 16 ÷ d² participants per group for 80% power at α = 0.05. For d = 0.8 that is 16 ÷ 0.64, or 25 per group.
Small effects need many more people, because the need grows with the square.
A team studies an effect of d = 0.4. They want 80% power at α = 0.05, using Lehr's rule of thumb.

reveal.text: Squaring 0.4 gives 0.16, and 16 ÷ 0.16 is the group size. Halve d and you need four times as many people per group.

steps.headline: A result that fails to replicate is weak evidence, whatever the original paper said.

lead.text: A replication repeats a study with fresh participants. The Open Science Collaboration repeated 100 psychology studies. Of the 97 originals that were significant, 35 replications were. Power posing and several other famous results also failed careful replications.
Small, lucky studies overstate effects. A fair repeat usually finds less.
Ego depletion is the claim that self-control runs down like fuel. Published studies averaged about d = 0.6. A preregistered replication across 23 laboratories tested 2,141 people.

reveal.text: A tiny d beside a published 0.6 is what overstated early estimates look like. The large, preregistered repeat is the better evidence.

lessons.orientation: Compute Cohen's d and the sample a study needs, then read failed replications as evidence.
lessons.reviewLabel: How big, and will it replicate?
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A training course lifts test scores by 6 points on average. In class A, scores usually vary by about 3 points either way. In class B they usually vary by about 30.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compute Cohen's d, estimate the sample a study needs, and read a failed replication as evidence rather than bad luck.

recap.keyIdea: An effect is only as big as it is large next to the spread, which is what d measures. Small studies miss real effects and overstate lucky ones, so one result needs repeating.

blocks.text: You divided a 6-point gain by a spread of 15 to get d = 0.4, and found that an effect that size needs 100 people per group. A multi-lab replication then gave d = 0.04, nowhere near the published 0.6.

recap.nextHook: Next, how to tell a real signal from noise when a judgement can go wrong in two ways.

lessons.title: Signal and noise

steps.headline: Every yes-or-no decision about a faint signal lands in one of four cells.

lead.text: On scans that contain a tumour, saying yes is a hit and saying no is a miss. On clear scans, saying yes is a false alarm and saying no is a correct rejection. The hit rate is hits divided by the signal trials.
Two of the four cells are errors, and they trade against each other.
A radiologist reviews 50 scans that contain a tumour. She reports a tumour on 40 of them.

reveal.text: You counted hits out of the scans that had a tumour, not out of every scan. Scans without a tumour belong to the false-alarm rate instead.

steps.headline: Sensitivity, d′, is the distance between the noise and signal curves, whatever the observer decides.

lead.text: Convert the hit rate and the false-alarm rate to z-scores, then subtract: d′ = z(H) − z(FA). Noisier scans pull the two curves together, so d′ falls, no matter what the observer chooses to say.
d′ rewards saying yes when the signal is there and no when it is not.

steps.headline: Find d′ when the hit rate has z = 1.28 and the false-alarm rate has z = −1.28.

workedSteps.text: Write the formula.
Substitute the two z-scores.
Calculate.

lead.text: A second observer sees the clearer scans. Her hit rate is 0.80, with z = 0.84. Her false-alarm rate is 0.20, with z = −0.84.

reveal.text: The false-alarm z-score is negative, so subtracting it adds its size. A good observer is high on hits and low on false alarms.

steps.headline: The criterion, c, measures how readily an observer says yes, and it is separate from sensitivity.

lead.text: The criterion is the line that decides when to say yes. c = −[z(H) + z(FA)] ÷ 2. It is zero midway between the curves, negative for a liberal observer and positive for a conservative one.
Training improves d′. Costs and rewards move c.
A baggage screener flags bags at the faintest hint of danger. Missing a weapon would be far worse than a delay.

reveal.text: The negative sign says she leans towards yes. The costs of a miss moved her criterion, not her skill.

lessons.orientation: Separate how well an observer can tell signal from noise (d′) from how willing they are to say yes.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two guards watch a car park. Guard A shouts “thief!” on all 10 nights a thief came, and on 9 of the 10 nights none did. Guard B shouts on 8 of the 10 thief nights and on 1 of the 10 quiet nights.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compute d′ to separate skill from willingness, and the criterion c that measures how readily an observer says yes.

recap.keyIdea: A hit rate mixes skill with willingness. d′ measures how well signal is told from noise, and the criterion c measures how readily the observer says yes.

blocks.text: You turned 40 hits from 50 tumour scans into a hit rate of 80%, and found d′ = 1.68 from z-scores of 0.84 and −0.84. A yes-prone screener with z(H) = 1.68 and z(FA) = 0 has c = −0.84.

recap.nextHook: Skill at noticing is only half of the story: how much of what you see is what you expect to see?

lessons.title: Where attention goes

steps.headline: Seeing needs attention, so something plainly visible can still go unnoticed.

lead.text: Selective attention lets you follow one stream and ignore the rest. In one famous study, viewers counted basketball passes and many never noticed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the game. This is inattentional blindness.
The object was in plain view. It was not attended, so it was not seen.
In a class demonstration, 30 people counted basketball passes. 14 of them failed to notice the person in the gorilla suit.

reveal.text: Nearly half missed it. Simons and Chabris reported 46% in the original study. In this class only 1 of 30 people who simply watched missed it.

steps.headline: Each change of task adds a switch cost while the mind reconfigures.

lead.text: Take two kinds of judgement: odd or even for digits (A), vowel or consonant for letters (B). Every trial takes some time, and every change from A to B or B to A adds a switch cost on top.
Total time = trials × time per trial + switches × switch cost.

steps.headline: Find the time for AABAB when each trial takes 400 ms and each switch adds 100 ms.

workedSteps.text: Five trials, each 400 ms.
Count the changes of task: A to B, B to A, A to B.
Each switch adds 100 ms.
Add the trial time and the switch time.

lead.text: Now use the digit and letter judgements. Each trial takes 600 ms, and each change of task adds 200 ms.

reveal.text: You counted seven changes in eight trials and added their cost to the trial time. Alternating is expensive because every trial after the first is a switch.

lead.text: Now compare the same eight judgements done in two blocks, AAAABBBB, with the alternating order. The trial times and the switch cost are as before.

reveal.text: Alternating loses 1,200 ms. Preparation shrinks switch costs but does not remove them, which is why answering messages while writing is slower than it feels.

lead.text: Watson and Strayer tested 200 people driving a simulator while doing a demanding memory-and-arithmetic task. Doing two demanding tasks usually means alternating between them.

reveal.text: Only 5, or 2.5%, showed no measurable cost. They are called supertaskers. Most people who believe they multitask well are among the other 97.5%.

lessons.orientation: Measure what selective attention misses and what switching between tasks costs.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You have eight cards to sort, each one a different kind of job. Four are maths sums and four are word puzzles. Each card takes the same time to do. You can do the sums first and the words after, or swap every card between sum and word.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say why attending to one thing hides another, and work out what switching between tasks costs you in time.

recap.keyIdea: Attention is selective, so unattended things can be missed even when visible, and every change of task adds a switch cost. Multitasking is mostly alternating.

blocks.text: You found that 14 of 30 counters, 46.7%, missed the gorilla. Alternating ABABABAB took 6,200 ms against 5,000 ms in blocks, a 1,200 ms loss, and only 2.5% of drivers showed no cost.

recap.nextHook: Switching costs hint that the mind holds only a little at once. How little?

lessons.title: Perception as inference

steps.headline: The brain combines cues by their reliability: the steadier a cue, the more weight it gets.

lead.text: A cue's reliability is 1 ÷ SD², where SD measures how much its readings wander. Its weight is its reliability divided by the total of both. The combined estimate is the weighted average of the readings.
Equal reliability gives equal weights, so two equally steady cues split the difference.
Sight says a block is 50 mm tall, with a standard deviation of 2 mm. Touch says 56 mm, with a standard deviation of 4 mm. Weight each cue by its reliability, 1 ÷ SD².

reveal.text: Sight carries 0.8 of the weight because its SD is half touch's. Ernst and Banks found that people combine sight and touch with weights close to these.

steps.headline: Combine a cue reading 20 (SD 1) with a cue reading 30 (SD 3).

workedSteps.text: Find each reliability, 1 ÷ SD².
Divide each by the total, 10 ÷ 9, to get the weights.
Weight the readings and add them.

lead.text: Add visual noise so that vision's SD rises to 4 mm while touch improves to 2 mm. The two readings stay the same, 50 mm for vision and 56 mm for touch.

reveal.text: Touch now carries 0.8 of the weight. The same two readings give a different answer because the brain tracks how trustworthy each reading is.

steps.headline: Combining independent cues gives an estimate sharper than either cue alone.

lead.text: The combined SD is 1 ÷ √(1/SD₁² + 1/SD₂²). For SDs of 5 and 12 mm it is about 4.6 mm, below both. A second cue always adds information, even a poor one.
The narrow curve in the explorer is that sharper estimate.
Two independent cues have standard deviations of 3 mm and 4 mm. Use the formula for the combined SD.

reveal.text: The combined SD is smaller than either cue alone. Two noisy cues, used together, beat the better of them.

lead.text: What you expect can act like one more cue. Expecting a line to be upright is like a cue reading 0°, with its own spread.

reveal.text: The expectation carries 0.9 of the weight, so you see the line as almost upright. Expectation treated like a cue is a prior, and perception shaped by it is top-down processing. A hollow mask seen from behind looks like an ordinary face for the same reason.

lessons.orientation: Combine noisy cues and prior expectations by their reliability, as the perceptual system appears to.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You look at a block in good light and judge it to be 50 mm tall. In thick gloves you feel it and guess 56 mm. Your eyes are far more reliable than your gloved fingers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll combine noisy cues by their reliability, and see expectation act as one more cue.

recap.keyIdea: The brain weights every cue, expectation included, by 1 ÷ SD². The combined estimate is sharper than any single cue.

blocks.text: You weighted sight and touch to get 51.2 mm, then 54.8 mm when the noise swapped sides. You also found a combined SD of 2.4 mm, and a line glimpsed at 10° seen as 1° because expectation carried most of the weight.

recap.nextHook: Perception is only the front door. What does the mind hold on to once it has seen something?

lessons.title: Holding it in mind

steps.headline: Short-term memory holds about four chunks, not seven separate items.

lead.text: Miller's 1956 estimate was seven items, plus or minus two. When rehearsal and grouping are prevented, the better estimate is about four chunks (Cowan, 2001). A chunk is a unit you already know.
The limit is on chunks, not on digits or letters.
Nine unrelated digits are read once. Each digit is its own chunk, and the capacity is four chunks.

reveal.text: Five digits overflow the store. Grouped in threes, the same nine digits would form three chunks, inside the limit.

steps.headline: Chunking groups items into units you already know, so the same limit holds more.

lead.text: A reader who knows the acronyms CD and TV sees those four letters as two chunks. Scramble them and each letter becomes its own chunk.
Chunking raises what you hold, not the limit itself.
A reader with a four-chunk capacity knows the acronyms FBI, BBC, NHS and USA.

reveal.text: Four acronym chunks hold 12 letters, where single letters would hold 4. Scramble the same letters and each one is its own chunk again.

lead.text: Chase and Simon showed a chess master and weaker players a real game position for five seconds. The master rebuilt far more of it, recalling pieces in meaningful groups. With random positions the advantage vanished.

reveal.text: The master's capacity is ordinary. The chunks are rich: five pieces in each.

steps.headline: Working memory has parts, and each part holds a different kind of material.

lead.text: Baddeley and Hitch split short-term storage into parts. A visuospatial sketchpad holds images and positions. An episodic buffer links them. A central executive directs attention among them. A fourth part holds speech-based material.
Interference is greatest between items held in the same part.
People recalled short lists of words in order. Some lists sounded alike, such as man, cat, map. Others did not, such as pit, day, cow.

reveal.text: The phonological loop holds speech-based material, so words that sound alike interfere with one another.

lessons.orientation: Estimate working-memory capacity in chunks and use knowledge to make the chunks bigger.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Read each list once, look away for ten seconds, then say it back. List A: 4 9 1 7 2 8 5 3 6. List B: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate how many chunks you can hold, and show how knowledge makes each chunk bigger.

recap.keyIdea: Working memory holds about four chunks, and a chunk is whatever you already know as a unit. Knowledge makes chunks bigger, so expertise raises what you hold without raising the limit.

blocks.text: You found that nine unrelated digits overflow a four-chunk store by 5, while chess pieces grouped five to a chunk let a master hold 20 pieces. You also matched similar-sounding words to the phonological loop.

recap.nextHook: What you hold for seconds is fragile. How fast does it fade once you stop thinking about it?

lessons.title: Forgetting and spaced retrieval

steps.headline: Forgetting is fast at first and slower later, and one curve can describe it.

lead.text: Ebbinghaus found this shape, and Murre and Dros reproduced it in 2015. We use R = 1/(1 + t/9S). Here R is predicted recall, and t is days since the last retrieval. S is stability: the days until R falls to 90%.
A bigger S means a flatter curve and slower forgetting.
A memory has a stability of S = 10 days. Use the curve R = 1/(1 + t/9S).

reveal.text: At 90 days, t ÷ 9S has reached 1, so recall has halved. A memory with S = 2 halves by day 18, five times sooner.

steps.headline: A successful review returns recall to near 100% and raises stability.

lead.text: Retrieving a memory resets the clock and flattens the curve. Reviewing at widening intervals is spaced, or distributed, practice. Cramming everything into one session is massed practice.
Each success multiplies stability, so the next gap can be longer.

steps.headline: Find predicted recall 15 days after a review that leaves stability at 5 days.

workedSteps.text: Find 9S.
Divide t by 9S.
Put it in the curve.
Read it as a percentage: 75%.

lead.text: A review on day 4 triples a memory's stability, from 2 days to 6 days. Now measure from that review.

reveal.text: Without the review, recall on day 17.5 would be about 51%. The review lifted it to 80% by making the curve flatter.

lead.text: Discere schedules reviews with FSRS. Each card has a stability. A review is due when predicted recall falls to the target of 90%.

reveal.text: Stability is defined as the days until recall reaches 90%, so the interval equals S. Each success raises S, so intervals expand. The current FSRS-6 curve has a flatter fitted tail but shares the 90% point.

lead.text: Roediger and Karpicke had students either reread a passage or practise recalling it. Five minutes later rereading looked better, 81% against 75%.

reveal.text: A week later the order flipped: 56% of idea units for recall practice against 42% for rereading. Effortful retrieval feels worse and lasts longer, which is why Discere asks before it shows.

model.setting: Recall after one week, per 100 idea units
Recall after one week, per 100 idea units

lessons.orientation: Read a forgetting curve and see how each successful retrieval flattens it, as Discere's scheduler assumes.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You learn 100 new words. A day later you still know 60 of them, so you have lost 40. Then you stop revising.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a forgetting curve and work out when a card is due after each successful review.

recap.keyIdea: Forgetting is fast at first and slows. Each successful retrieval raises stability, so reviews can be spaced further apart, and practising recall beats rereading for lasting memory.

blocks.text: You found that a memory with stability 10 days is predicted to fall to 50% by day 90, and that a review on day 4 lifted recall on day 17.5 from about 51% to 80%. A week on, recall practice led rereading by 14 points.

recap.nextHook: Memory fades with time. It also bends to what has been learned before, and that can be learned unintentionally.

lessons.title: Conditioning and reinforcement

steps.headline: Each pairing closes a share of the gap between what the signal predicts now and the most it can predict.

lead.text: Pavlov's dogs came to salivate at a bell that had preceded food. The Rescorla–Wagner rule says associative strength V rises on each pairing by ΔV = rate × (λ − V), where λ is the maximum V can reach.
Each step is smaller than the last, because there is less left to learn.
A bell is paired with food twice. The rate is 0.3, the maximum is 1, and V starts at 0.

reveal.text: The first pairing takes V from 0 to 0.3. The second adds only 0.3 of the remaining gap, so it is smaller.

steps.headline: A bell has V = 0.5. Find V after one trial with the bell alone, at a rate of 0.2.

workedSteps.text: With no food, the maximum λ is 0.
Apply the rule.
Add the change to V.

lead.text: Now the rate is 0.5 and the maximum is 1 with food. The bell is paired with food twice, then presented alone once. When the bell is alone, the maximum is 0.

reveal.text: The model treats a bell-alone trial as unlearning. Yet responding can return after a rest, which is called spontaneous recovery. Extinction adds new learning more than it erases the old.

steps.headline: In operant conditioning a consequence follows a behaviour and makes it more or less likely.

lead.text: Positive means something is added. Negative means something is removed. Reinforcement makes the behaviour more likely, and punishment makes it less likely.
Ask two questions: was something added or removed, and did the behaviour rise or fall?
A pigeon pecks a key on a fixed-ratio 5 schedule: every fifth peck is rewarded.

reveal.text: A variable-ratio schedule that averages five can pay out the same six times. It rewards an unpredictable number of responses, so responding stays high and extinction is slow, as slot machines show.

lead.text: On a fixed-interval schedule, the first response after a set time is rewarded. A rat on a 10-second interval presses every 3 seconds for a minute.

reveal.text: Rewards land at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 seconds. Pressing faster would not earn more. Animals pause after each reward and speed up near the deadline.

lessons.orientation: Track how a signal gains associative strength and how reinforcement schedules shape behaviour.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A dog hears a bell just before it is fed, every time. After a few days it starts to drool at the bell alone.

intro.promise: By the end you'll track how a signal gains strength with each pairing, and name the consequence or schedule behind a pattern of behaviour.

recap.keyIdea: Learning from pairings closes a share of the remaining gap each time, so gains shrink. Consequences and reward schedules then shape behaviour, and unpredictable schedules resist extinction best.

blocks.text: You found that two pairings at a rate of 0.3 give V = 0.51, and that a bell alone then pulls V back towards zero. Thirty pecks on a fixed-ratio 5 schedule earned 6 rewards, and a fixed 10-second interval allowed only 5.

recap.nextHook: Behaviour follows its consequences. Judgement follows what comes to mind first, and that is where the next lesson goes.

lessons.title: Base rates and Bayes

steps.headline: Natural frequencies turn percentages into counts of people, which makes a test result easy to read.

lead.text: Picture 1,000 people. If 2% have a condition, that is 20 people. If a test catches half of them, that is 10 true positives. Counting people avoids multiplying percentages in your head.
A percentage of a group is a number of people. Work with the number.
1,000 people are screened for a disease that 1% have. The test flags 90% of those who have it, so there are 9 true positives. It also wrongly flags 10% of people who do not have the disease.

reveal.text: False positives outnumber the true positives by more than ten to one. The healthy group is large, so even a small error rate flags many people.

steps.headline: The chance that a positive result is right is the true positives divided by all positives.

lead.text: A positive result puts you among everyone the test flagged: the true positives plus the false positives. Most people answer near the test's hit rate instead. Ignoring how rare the condition is, is base-rate neglect.
Ask who is in the flagged group, and how many of them have the condition.

steps.headline: 500 people are tested; 10% have the disease. The test flags 60% of cases and 20% of healthy people. What share of positives are right?

workedSteps.text: Split the people into those with and without the disease.
Count the true positives and the false positives.
Divide the true positives by all positives.

lead.text: Of 1,000 people, 9 true positives and 99 false positives test positive. A person is among the flagged.

reveal.text: Only 9 of the 108 flagged people have the disease. Answering with the test's 90% hit rate would be badly wrong.

lead.text: Use the same test, with a 90% hit rate and a 10% false-alarm rate, in a clinic where 10% of 1,000 people have the disease.

reveal.text: Nothing about the test changed, yet a positive now means far more. The meaning of a result depends on who is being tested.

lead.text: In a city, 20% of cabs are blue and the rest green. A witness names colours correctly 75% of the time. Picture 1,000 cabs: 200 blue and 800 green.

reveal.text: A witness who names colours reliably is still more likely wrong than right here, because green cabs are so much more common.

lessons.orientation: Turn a test result into a probability by counting people, so the base rate cannot be ignored.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: At an airport, 1,000 bags are scanned and 2 of them hold a banned item. The scanner beeps for both of those bags. It also beeps for 98 of the 998 bags that hold nothing banned.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a test result into a probability by counting people, and see why a rare condition makes most positives wrong.

recap.keyIdea: The chance that a positive result is right is true positives divided by all positives. When the condition is rare, false positives swamp the true ones, so ignoring the base rate misleads.

blocks.text: You counted 9 true positives against 99 false positives, so a positive meant 8.3%, not 90%. In the clinic at 10% prevalence the same test gave 50%, and the witness who named blue was right only 42.9% of the time.

recap.nextHook: Counting people fixes this error. Other errors come from the first number we meet, true or not.

lessons.title: Anchors and fast thinking

steps.headline: An anchor is a number you meet first, and it pulls later estimates towards it even when it is plainly irrelevant.

lead.text: Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to stop at 10 or 65. They then asked what percentage of United Nations members were African countries. Those who saw the higher number guessed higher.
Anchoring bias is the pull of a starting number on an estimate, even a number known to be random.
After the wheel stopped on 10, the median estimate was 25%. After it stopped on 65, the median estimate was 45%.

reveal.text: The number was plainly irrelevant, yet it moved the typical estimate by that gap.

model.quantity: Share of UN members that are African countries (%)
Estimated age of an oak tree (years)

steps.headline: The anchoring index divides the gap between median estimates by the gap between anchors.

lead.text: An index of 0 means the anchor was ignored. An index of 1 means estimates moved as far as the anchors did. Anchors of 0 and 100 with medians of 30 and 50 give 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2.
The index measures how much of the anchors' gap shows up in the estimates.

steps.headline: Find the anchoring index for anchors of 10 and 70 with median estimates of 30 and 51.

workedSteps.text: Find the gap between the medians.
Find the gap between the anchors.
Divide the first gap by the second.

model.quantity: Estimated age of an oak tree (years)
Share of UN members that are African countries (%)

lead.text: Anchors of 20 and 80 were used, and the median estimates of an oak tree's age were 35 and 59 years.

reveal.text: Estimates moved 0.4 of the way between the anchors. Even random starting numbers pull estimates a long way.

lead.text: Are there more English words that start with k, or more that have k as the third letter? Most people say start. Now count.

reveal.text: Words with k third are about twice as common, yet words that start with k are easier to call to mind. Judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind is the availability heuristic.

model.setting: Illustrative sample of 600 words containing k

lead.text: A bat and a ball cost £1.10 together. The bat costs £1.00 more than the ball.

reveal.text: The answer that springs to mind, 10p, would make the total £1.20. Kahneman calls the quick answer System 1 and the check System 2. These are names for fast and deliberate thinking, not two brain organs. Intuition is often right; the skill is knowing when to check.

model.setting: Illustrative group answering the bat-and-ball problem
Illustrative group told to verify the total

lessons.orientation: Measure the pull of an anchor and the bias of availability, then check a fast intuition with a slow one.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: One shop shows a jacket as “was £200, now £120”. Another shop sells the same jacket at £120, with no other price shown.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how far an anchor pulls an estimate, and see how ease of recall and quick answers can mislead.

recap.keyIdea: The first number you meet pulls your estimate, and what comes to mind easily feels common. Fast intuition is often right, so the skill is checking it when the stakes call for it.

blocks.text: You found that a random wheel moved median estimates by 20 points, an anchoring index of 0.4 for the tree ages, and that only a third of k-words start with k. The bat and ball cost 5p, not the 10p that springs to mind.

recap.nextHook: Fast thinking is shaped by what is in front of us. Next: how other people's behaviour shapes our own.

lessons.title: Conformity, obedience and bystanders

steps.headline: Conformity is giving the group's answer even when your own eyes say otherwise.

lead.text: Asch had people match line lengths after several confederates gave the same wrong answer. Alone, people erred on under 1% of judgements. A critical answer is one given after the majority has spoken wrongly.
To measure conformity, count the critical answers that follow the wrong majority.
In a line-judgement replication, 18 people each gave 12 critical answers. Of all those answers, 72 followed the wrong majority.

reveal.text: About a third of critical answers went along, as Asch found. Most answers stayed independent, and about a quarter of people never yielded.

model.setting: Asch's majority condition, about 37 in every 100 critical answers
Asch's majority condition, about 75 in every 100 people

steps.headline: Obedience is following an authority's instruction, and it weakens as the victim gets closer.

lead.text: In Milgram's 1963 study, participants told to shock a learner for errors were urged on by an experimenter. The learner was an actor and no shocks were real. In the same room, 16 of 40 went on to the end.
Obedience is measured by the share who go on to the final 450-volt switch.
In Milgram's baseline condition, 26 of 40 participants continued to the final 450-volt switch.

reveal.text: Most continued, though the learner was an actor and no shocks were real. Few people predicted that before the study.

lead.text: In the touch-proximity condition, the participant had to press the learner's hand onto a shock plate. 12 of 40 continued to the end.

reveal.text: Closeness weakened obedience but did not remove it. Burger's 2009 partial replication stopped at 150 volts: 70% were willing to continue, against 82.5% in Milgram's comparable condition. Gina Perry's archives found that experimenters sometimes left the script and many participants doubted the shocks. Obedience is real; the exact percentages depend on setting and belief.

steps.headline: More witnesses spread responsibility, so each person is less likely to act.

lead.text: Darley and Latané staged a seizure over an intercom. 85% of those who thought they alone heard it helped, against 31% who thought four others heard. If n people each act independently with chance p, at least one acts with chance 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ.
More people give more chances, but each person's own chance can fall.
Five bystanders each independently act with probability 0.2.

reveal.text: Even a low chance each gives a fair chance that someone acts. The famous 38 silent witnesses to the Genovese murder is largely a myth. CCTV of 219 real street conflicts showed that someone intervened in 91%.

lessons.orientation: Read the classic social-influence studies by their numbers, together with what replications and critics found.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: On an empty station platform, one person sees a stranger collapse. On a crowded platform, forty people see the same thing.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read the classic conformity, obedience and bystander results as rates and probabilities, and say what critics added.

recap.keyIdea: Groups and authority shift behaviour by measurable amounts, and a bystander's chance of acting falls as the crowd grows. The percentages depend on the setting, and replications and archives refine them.

blocks.text: You found that 72 of 216 critical answers conformed, 33.3%, and that 26 of 40 obeyed to 450 volts. Obedience fell by 35 points when the participant had to touch the victim, and five bystanders at 0.2 each give 67.2%.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course. You can now read a study's numbers and ask what else could explain them.

questions.prompt: Sleep and reaction time correlate at r = −0.6. What percentage of the variation in reaction time do they share?
hints: The shared share of variation comes from squaring r.
A negative number squared is positive.
Square 0.6 and convert the decimal to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Shared variance is r² = (−0.6)² = 0.36, so 36%. Squaring removes the sign.

questions.onCorrect: Squaring r removes the sign: (−0.6)² gives the shared share, a little over a third of the variation.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads r as a percentage. The shared share comes from squaring r.
That is the right square written as a decimal. The question asks for a percentage.
That is the share left over. The question asks how much is shared.

questions.prompt: Across towns, those with more libraries also have more burglaries. Population size drives both. What do psychologists call a variable like population that produces a misleading correlation?
hints: It is a hidden third variable that affects both measured variables.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Population is a confound: a third variable that drives both measures.

questions.onCorrect: A confound drives both measures, so they move together without either causing the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Reverse causation flips the arrow between two measures. Here a separate variable sits behind both.

questions.prompt: Across a sample, weekly exercise and mood correlate at r = 0.3. Which explanation has the arrow running from mood to exercise?
hints: Reverse causation flips which variable is the cause.

acceptedIdeas: People in a better mood are more likely to go out and exercise
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reverse causation runs the arrow from mood to exercise. Sunny weather would be a confound, and endorphins assume the original direction.

choices.label: People in a better mood are more likely to go out and exercise
Exercise raises mood by releasing endorphins
Sunny weather increases both exercise and mood

questions.onCorrect: When the arrow runs from mood to exercise, being in a good mood leads to more exercise. The correlation alone cannot rule it out.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the arrow running from exercise to mood, the direction the data seem to suggest.
That puts a third variable behind both measures. No arrow runs between exercise and mood.

questions.prompt: 6 of 20 full-moon shifts were busy, and 30 of 100 other shifts were busy. By how many percentage points does the busy rate differ between the two kinds of shift?
hints: Turn each count into a rate before comparing.
Divide busy shifts by all shifts in each group.
Subtract one rate from the other.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6/20 = 30% and 30/100 = 30%, so the difference is 0 percentage points. The remembered link is an illusory correlation.

questions.onCorrect: Both groups were busy at the same rate. The vivid full-moon nights were memorable, not more frequent.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts raw counts, but the groups differ in size. Turn each into a rate first.
That compares the quiet shifts, which are different in number. Compare rates, not counts.

questions.prompt: Daily screen time and sleep quality correlate at r = −0.3. What percentage of the variation in sleep quality is shared with screen time?
hints: Use the square of the correlation coefficient.
The minus sign disappears when you square.
Square 0.3 and convert to a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: r² = 0.3² = 0.09, so 9%. A modest correlation leaves 91% of the variation to other causes.

questions.onCorrect: Square r and the sign drops out. A modest correlation shares only a small slice of the variation.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads r as a percentage. Square it first.
That is the share left over, not the share they have in common.

questions.prompt: A researcher records 'aggression' as the number of seconds a participant holds down a button that blasts noise at an opponent. What do we call a definition that turns a concept into a precise measurement like this?
hints: The definition tells you the operation used to measure the concept.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is an operational definition: it states exactly how aggression will be measured.

questions.onCorrect: An operational definition says exactly how a concept is measured, so anyone could repeat the measurement.

misconceptions.feedback: Those name the variable set and the variable measured. This asks what turns a concept into a measurement.

questions.prompt: How many hours a week higher is the programme group's average exercise than the other group's, before the programme starts?
hints: Find each group's mean separately.
Add the four values in a group and divide by four.
Subtract the comparison group's mean from the programme group's mean.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Programme mean = (9 + 8 + 8 + 7)/4 = 8; other mean = (3 + 2 + 2 + 1)/4 = 2; the head start is 6 hours.

questions.onCorrect: Each group's mean is its total divided by four. The joiners' head start is a confound built in by choice.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the programme group's own average. The question asks how far ahead it is of the other group.
That compares totals, and both groups have four people. Compare the averages instead.

questions.prompt: Random assignment gives every participant an equal what of being placed in each condition? Answer in one word.
hints: Think of a coin toss deciding each person's group.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An equal chance: assignment depends on the draw, never on the person.

questions.onCorrect: Assignment depends on the draw, never on the person, so no trait can decide who gets the programme.

misconceptions.feedback: Choosing is self-selection. Random assignment takes the choice away.

questions.prompt: Is resting heart rate the independent or the dependent variable?
hints: Ask which variable the researchers set and which they measure.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Resting heart rate is the dependent variable: it is measured to see the programme's effect.

questions.onCorrect: Resting heart rate is measured afterwards to see the programme's effect, so it depends on the condition.

misconceptions.feedback: The independent variable is the one the researchers set. Resting heart rate is measured after the condition is set.

questions.prompt: In a drug trial the drug group improves by 12 points and the placebo group by 8 points. How many points of improvement can be attributed to the drug's active ingredient?
hints: The placebo group improves without any active ingredient.
Remove the improvement that both groups share.
Subtract the placebo improvement from the drug improvement.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 8 = 4 points. The placebo group shows how much improvement expectation and time alone produce.

questions.onCorrect: Remove what both groups share. The placebo group shows what expectation and time produce alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the drug group's whole improvement, including what expectation alone produces.
That is the improvement without the active ingredient. Ask what the drug added beyond it.
Adding the groups mixes the two responses together. You need what is left after removing the shared part.

questions.prompt: A random draw puts people with prior fitness scores 4, 6, 5 and 7 in the treatment group, and 6, 5, 4 and 5 in the control group. What is the treatment mean minus the control mean?
hints: Find the mean of each group of four.
The treatment scores add to 22.
Subtract the control mean from the treatment mean.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Treatment mean = 22/4 = 5.5; control mean = 20/4 = 5; the chance gap is 0.5.

questions.onCorrect: Each mean is its total divided by four. The chance gap is small, as random assignment leads you to expect.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the treatment group's own mean. Subtract the control group's mean from it.
Check the order. The question asks for the treatment mean minus the control mean.

questions.prompt: In a trial, neither the participants nor the researchers who measure them know who received the real treatment. What is this design called?
hints: Count how many parties are kept unaware.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a double-blind design: both sides are kept unaware of the conditions.

questions.onCorrect: Both sides are kept unaware of the conditions, so neither expectation nor measuring can lean toward the treatment.

misconceptions.feedback: A single-blind design keeps only one party unaware. Count how many parties are unaware here.

questions.prompt: What is Cohen's d?
hints: Cohen's d is a difference measured in standard deviations.
Find the difference between the two means.
Divide that difference by 15.
questions.onCorrect: d is the difference between means measured in standard deviations: a gain of 6 beside a spread of 15.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference. Cohen's d measures it against the spread.
That divides the spread by the difference. d divides the difference by the spread.

questions.prompt: Two equal-sized groups have means 40 and 46.5 with standard deviations 7 and 17. Using the pooled SD √[(SD₁² + SD₂²)/2], what is Cohen's d?
hints: Square each standard deviation before averaging.
Average 49 and 289, then take the square root.
Divide the 6.5-point difference by the pooled SD.
questions.onCorrect: Pool the spreads from their squares, then divide the difference by that pooled SD.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the plain average of the two SDs. Pool the spreads through their squares.
That is the raw difference. Divide it by the pooled spread.

questions.prompt: How many participants per group does the study need?
hints: Square the effect size first.
0.4 squared is 0.16.
Divide 16 by the squared effect size.
questions.onCorrect: The need grows with 1 ÷ d²: for this effect, 16 divided by the square of d.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by d. The rule divides by d squared.
That is the top of the fraction. Divide it by d squared.

questions.prompt: A replication finds means of 50.4 (depleted) and 50.0 (control), both with standard deviation 10. What is Cohen's d?
hints: Divide the difference between means by the standard deviation.
The difference between the means is under one point.
Divide 0.4 by 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d = (50.4 − 50.0)/10 = 0.04, close to zero and far below the published average of about 0.6.

questions.onCorrect: The means differ by well under a tenth of a standard deviation, so the published effect did not hold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference in points. Divide it by the standard deviation.
That divides the SD by the difference. d divides the difference by the SD.

questions.prompt: Of 97 original studies with significant results, 35 replications were significant. What percentage replicated? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide the successful replications by the studies attempted.
Use 97 as the denominator, since only significant originals count.
Convert 35/97 to a percentage and round to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: Only the 97 significant originals count. The replications that succeeded, over that base, give about a third.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of studies that replicated. The question asks for a percentage.
That is the share that did not replicate. The question asks for the share that did.

questions.prompt: Which claim failed a large preregistered replication and should be treated as a cautionary case, not established fact?
hints: Two of the options are definitions or arithmetic; one is an empirical claim.

acceptedIdeas: Holding a power pose for two minutes raises testosterone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ranehill and colleagues (2015) found no hormonal effect of power poses in 200 people. The other two statements are mathematical facts.

choices.label: Holding a power pose for two minutes raises testosterone
Random assignment balances groups on average
Squaring r gives the shared variance

questions.onCorrect: Power posing's hormone effect failed a large replication. Arithmetic facts and balancing by chance are not claims that can fail that way.

misconceptions.feedback: Random assignment balancing groups on average is a property of chance, not a finding that was overturned.
Squaring r is arithmetic, so it cannot fail a replication.

questions.prompt: What is the hit rate as a percentage?
hints: A hit is a yes on a trial where the signal is present.
Divide by the number of scans with a tumour, not all scans.
Convert 40/50 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The hit rate is hits divided by signal trials, so only scans with a tumour count in the denominator.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of hits. Turn it into a share of the scans that had a tumour.
That is the share of tumour scans she missed. The hit rate is the share she caught.
That is the rate as a decimal. The question asks for a percentage.

questions.prompt: What is d′?
hints: d′ subtracts the false-alarm z-score from the hit z-score.
Subtracting a negative number adds its size.
Calculate 0.84 + 0.84.
questions.onCorrect: d′ = z(H) − z(FA), and subtracting a negative z-score adds its size.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats both z-scores as having the same sign. The false-alarm z-score is negative.
That is only one of the two z-scores. d′ combines both.

questions.prompt: On the same scans, a liberal observer has hit rate 0.954 (z = 1.68) and false-alarm rate 0.50 (z = 0). What is this observer's d′?
hints: Use the same formula as before with the new z-scores.
The z-score of a 0.50 rate is zero.
Subtract the false-alarm z-score from the hit z-score.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d′ = 1.68 − 0 = 1.68. Sensitivity is unchanged; only the criterion moved.

questions.onCorrect: Moving the criterion changed both rates but not the curves, so d′ stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the larger z-score from itself. Use z(H) − z(FA) with these values.
That halves the difference. d′ is the difference itself.

questions.prompt: A baggage screener has z(H) = 1.68 and z(FA) = 0. What is her criterion location c = −[z(H) + z(FA)]/2?
hints: Add the two z-scores first.
Halve the sum.
Keep the minus sign in front of the bracket.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: c = −(1.68 + 0)/2 = −0.84. A negative c means a bias towards saying yes.

questions.onCorrect: A negative c means a bias towards yes. Halve the sum of the z-scores and keep the minus sign.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. A screener who leans towards yes has a c below zero.
That leaves out the halving. Divide the sum by two.

questions.prompt: A lifeguard spots swimmers in difficulty with hit rate 0.69 (z = 0.50) and raises false alarms at rate 0.07 (z = −1.48). What is d′?
hints: Subtract z(FA) from z(H).
The false-alarm z-score is negative.
Add 0.50 and 1.48.
questions.onCorrect: Subtract z(FA) from z(H). The false-alarm z-score is negative, so d′ is the sum of their sizes.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the sizes. The false-alarm z-score is negative, so subtracting it adds.
That is only the false-alarm z-score's size. d′ also uses the hit z-score.

questions.prompt: Lowering the criterion so an observer says yes more often increases hits. Which other outcome, on trials with no signal, does it also increase?
hints: Think about the yes responses on trials with no signal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It also increases false alarms: more yes responses when no signal is present.

questions.onCorrect: A lower criterion means more yes answers everywhere, including false alarms on noise trials.

misconceptions.feedback: Lowering the criterion reduces misses. Think about trials with no signal at all.
More yes answers means fewer correct rejections, not more.

questions.prompt: What percentage missed it? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide the number who missed it by the number watching.
The denominator is 30.
Convert 14/30 to a percentage and round to one decimal place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 14/30 = 0.4667, or 46.7%, close to the 46% Simons and Chabris reported.

questions.onCorrect: Divide those who missed it by all who watched: nearly half failed to notice something in plain view.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of people who missed it. Turn it into a percentage of everyone watching.
That is the share who noticed it. The question asks for the share who missed it.

questions.prompt: How long does the sequence ABABABAB take in total, in milliseconds?
hints: Count the places where the letter changes.
Every trial costs 600 ms; each switch adds 200 ms.
Add 8 × 600 to the number of switches × 200.
questions.onCorrect: Trial time plus switch time: eight trials, and a switch before every trial except the first.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the trials. Each change of task adds more.
Eight trials make only seven changes. Count the gaps where the task changes.

questions.prompt: How many milliseconds longer does ABABABAB take than AAAABBBB?
hints: Both sequences have eight trials, so only switches differ.
Count the switches in each sequence.
Multiply the difference in switches by 200 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ABABABAB has 7 switches and AAAABBBB has 1; the extra 6 switches cost 6 × 200 = 1,200 ms.

questions.onCorrect: Both have eight trials, so only the switches differ: six more switches, each at the same cost.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cost of one switch. How many more switches does the alternating order have?
That is the whole switch cost of the alternating order. The blocked order has a switch too.

questions.prompt: In the study, 5 of 200 drivers showed no cost from doing a demanding task while driving. What percentage is that?
hints: Divide the supertaskers by the total tested.
The total is 200.
Convert 5/200 to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Five in two hundred is a very small share: nearly everyone paid a cost for doing two things.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of drivers. Turn it into a percentage of all those tested.
That is the share who showed a cost. The question asks about those who showed none.

questions.prompt: Each trial takes 500 ms and each change of task adds 150 ms. How long does AABBAABB take, in milliseconds?
hints: Look for each place where A is followed by B or B by A.
There are eight trials at 500 ms each.
Add the switch costs to 4,000 ms.
questions.onCorrect: Trial time plus switch time, with only the changes of task counted as switches.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the trials. Add the cost of each change of task.
Read the sequence again. It changes task fewer times than that.

questions.prompt: An observer concentrating on a task fails to see a clearly visible but unexpected object. What is this failure called?
hints: It is a kind of blindness caused by where attention was directed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inattentional blindness: the object was visible but not attended.

questions.onCorrect: The object was visible but not attended, so it went unseen. That is inattentional blindness.

misconceptions.feedback: Change blindness is missing a change between two views. Here the object was never attended.

questions.prompt: What is the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: Reliability is one over the variance, 1/SD².
Vision's share is its reliability divided by the sum of both.
Multiply each reading by its share and add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Weights 1/4 and 1/16 give vision 0.25/0.3125 = 0.8; estimate = 0.8 × 50 + 0.2 × 56 = 51.2 mm.

questions.onCorrect: Weights follow 1 ÷ SD², so the steadier cue counts for more than the midpoint would give it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That gives the larger weight to touch, but touch is the less reliable cue here.

questions.prompt: What is the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: The more reliable cue now is touch.
Combine 0.2 of the vision reading with the rest from touch.
questions.onCorrect: Touch is now the steadier cue, so it carries most of the weight and pulls the estimate towards its reading.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That uses the earlier weights. The steadier cue has changed.

questions.prompt: What is the standard deviation of the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: Add the two reliabilities 1/9 and 1/16.
Use the common denominator 144.
Take one over the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: Add the reliabilities, then invert: the combined SD sits below both cues.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of the two SDs. Combining cues does better than averaging.
That adds the squares of the SDs. The formula adds the reliabilities, 1 ÷ SD².

questions.prompt: You expect a line to be upright at 0° (SD 1°). You glimpse it at 10° (SD 3°). Combining expectation and glimpse by reliability, what tilt do you perceive, in degrees?
hints: Treat the expectation as a cue with its own SD.
The expectation's weight is 1/(1 + 1/9).
Only the glimpse's share multiplies a non-zero reading.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliabilities 1 and 1/9 give the expectation weight 0.9; perceived tilt = 0.9 × 0 + 0.1 × 10 = 1°.

questions.onCorrect: The steadier expectation carries most of the weight, so what you see is pulled almost to upright.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the midpoint of expectation and glimpse. The steadier one should count for more.
That gives the larger weight to the glimpse, but the expectation is the steadier cue.

questions.prompt: Hearing places a voice 10° to the right (SD 8°); vision places the moving lips at 0° (SD 4°). Where is the voice heard, in degrees to the right?
hints: Compute 1/SD² for each sense.
Hearing's weight is its reliability over the total.
Multiply that weight by 10°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliabilities 1/64 and 1/16 give hearing weight (1/64)/(5/64) = 0.2; location = 0.2 × 10 = 2°. Vision captures the sound, as in ventriloquism.

questions.onCorrect: Hearing is the less reliable sense, so vision pulls the heard location towards the lips. This is the ventriloquist effect.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the midpoint. Vision is steadier, so it should count for more.
That gives most of the weight to hearing, the less reliable sense.

questions.prompt: Perception guided by knowledge and expectation, rather than built only from incoming sensory features, is called what kind of processing?
hints: It runs in the opposite direction to bottom-up processing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Top-down processing: knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived.

questions.onCorrect: Knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived. That is top-down, the reverse of building from features.

misconceptions.feedback: Bottom-up builds perception from the incoming features alone. This asks for the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: How many digits exceed the limit?
hints: Each separate digit counts as one chunk.
Compare the number of chunks with the capacity.
Subtract the capacity from the number of digits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves 9 − 4 = 5 beyond the limit.

questions.onCorrect: Nine chunks against a capacity of four leaves the difference beyond the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every digit. Only those beyond what the store can hold exceed the limit.
That is the capacity. The question asks how many are over it.

questions.prompt: How many more letters can they hold by chunking than by storing one letter per chunk?
hints: Find how many letters fit when each chunk is an acronym.
Find how many fit when each chunk is one letter.
Subtract the second from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four acronym chunks hold 12 letters; four single-letter chunks hold 4; the gain is 8.

questions.onCorrect: Each chunk holds a whole acronym, so the same four chunks carry far more letters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number held by chunking. The question asks for the extra over one letter per chunk.
That is how many letters fit without chunking. Find the gain over that.

questions.prompt: A chess master recalls a 20-piece position as 4 chunks. On average, how many pieces are in each chunk?
hints: Average means total pieces shared equally across chunks.
There are 20 pieces in the position.
Divide by the number of chunks.
questions.onCorrect: The master's chunks are rich, with several pieces in each. Capacity stays ordinary.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of chunks. The question asks how many pieces each one holds.
That subtracts instead of sharing the pieces out equally.

questions.prompt: Lists of similar-sounding words are harder to recall in order. Which part of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model does this point to?
hints: The interference comes from sound.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The phonological loop stores speech-based codes, so similar sounds interfere with one another.

choices.label: Phonological loop
Visuospatial sketchpad
Central executive
Episodic buffer

questions.onCorrect: Similar sounds interfere in the speech-based store, so similar-sounding words are recalled worse.

misconceptions.feedback: The sketchpad holds images and positions, not sound.
The central executive directs attention. It does not store sound.
The episodic buffer links the other parts. The interference here comes from sound.

questions.prompt: A 16-digit card number is printed in groups of four. If each group becomes one chunk, how many chunks must be held?
hints: Each printed group becomes a single chunk.
Find how many groups of four make 16.
Divide 16 by the group size.
questions.onCorrect: Each printed group becomes one chunk, so sixteen digits become only a few chunks.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the digits. Each group of four is one chunk.
That is the number of digits left after one group. Divide the digits by the size of a group.

questions.prompt: What is the strategy of organising items into meaningful groups so more fits in short-term memory called?
hints: The groups are called chunks.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chunking: grouping items into units already known from long-term memory.

questions.onCorrect: Chunking groups items into units already known, so more fits within the same limit.

misconceptions.feedback: Rehearsal repeats items. The strategy asked about groups them into units.

questions.prompt: What percentage recall does the curve predict 90 days after learning?
hints: Compute 9S first.
Divide t by 9S.
Substitute into 1/(1 + t/9S) and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Divide the days by 9S and put it in the curve: here the ratio reaches one and recall has halved.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of days. Put t ÷ 9S into the curve to get a percentage.
That divides t by S. The curve divides by nine times S.

questions.prompt: What percentage recall is predicted 13.5 days after that review?
hints: Multiply the stability by 9.
Divide 13.5 by that product.
Take one over one plus your answer.
questions.onCorrect: The review raised stability, so 9S is bigger and t ÷ 9S is smaller: recall stays high.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops after t ÷ 9S. Put it in the curve to get recall.
That is the share forgotten. The question asks for the share recalled.

questions.prompt: A card has stability 12 days. If reviews are scheduled for when predicted recall falls to 90%, how many days after its last review is it due?
hints: Recall the definition of stability.
The 90% target matches that definition exactly.
The interval equals the stability.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Stability is defined as the interval at which predicted recall reaches 90%, so the card is due in 12 days.

questions.onCorrect: Stability is the days to reach the 90% target, so the card is due after that many days.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the target recall, not a number of days.
That multiplies by nine. The definition of S already includes the 90% target.

questions.prompt: A week after studying, students who practised recall remembered 56% of idea units and students who reread remembered 42%. How many percentage points higher was recall practice?
hints: Compare the two one-week scores.
Percentage points are a plain difference of percentages.
Subtract the rereading score from the recall-practice score.
questions.onCorrect: Recall practice looked worse early but lasted longer. The gap is a plain difference of the two scores.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two scores. The question asks how far apart they are.
Percentage points are a difference, not a sum.

questions.prompt: A memory has stability S = 4 days. Using R = 1/(1 + t/9S), what percentage recall is predicted 108 days after learning?
hints: Multiply S by 9.
Divide 108 by that result.
Take one over one plus the quotient.
questions.onCorrect: Divide the days by 9S, then put the ratio in the curve. A longer wait with smaller stability leaves less recall.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share forgotten. The question asks for the share still recalled.
That is t ÷ 9S, not recall. Put it into the curve.

questions.prompt: Studying in short sessions spread over days, rather than one long session, is called what kind of practice?
hints: It is the opposite of massed practice, or cramming.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Distributed, or spaced, practice.

questions.onCorrect: Spreading study over days is distributed, or spaced, practice, the opposite of cramming.

misconceptions.feedback: Massed practice is one long session. The question asks about study spread across days.

questions.prompt: What is V after two pairings?
hints: Work one trial at a time.
The first trial adds 0.3 × (1 − 0).
On trial two the remaining gap is 1 − 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: The second step closes the same share of a smaller gap, so V grows more slowly the more it has.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the first step twice. The second step is smaller because less gap is left.
That is the value after only the first pairing.

questions.prompt: Starting from V = 0, what is the final V?
hints: Compute the two pairings first.
On the bell-alone trial the target is 0.
Move V halfway towards 0 from its value after two pairings.
questions.onCorrect: On the bell-alone trial V moves a share of the way towards 0: unlearning that is partial, not total.

misconceptions.feedback: That is V before the bell-alone trial. The final trial changes it.
That wipes out all learning. The rule moves V only part of the way to the target.

questions.prompt: It makes 30 pecks. How many rewards does it earn?
hints: Fixed ratio 5 means a fixed number of responses per reward.
Count how many complete sets of five fit in 30.
Divide 30 by 5.
questions.onCorrect: Every fifth response pays, so divide the responses by the ratio.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies. Each reward needs five responses, so divide instead.
That subtracts the ratio once. Count how many sets of five fit in the total.

questions.prompt: On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, a rat presses every 3 seconds for 60 seconds. The first press at least 10 s after the previous reward is rewarded. How many rewards does it earn?
hints: The first press at or after 10 s is at 12 s.
The next must come at least 10 s after 12 s.
Keep stepping until 60 s and count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rewarded presses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.

questions.onCorrect: Only presses can be rewarded, and presses fall every 3 seconds, so each reward lands a little after the interval.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the time by the interval. A reward needs a press, and presses come every 3 seconds.
That is the number of presses, not the number of rewards.

questions.prompt: A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win in twenty. Which reinforcement schedule is this?
hints: Decide whether rewards depend on time or on the number of responses, and whether that number is predictable.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Variable ratio: rewards follow an unpredictable number of responses.

questions.onCorrect: Rewards after an unpredictable number of responses form a variable-ratio schedule, the hardest to extinguish.

misconceptions.feedback: Fixed means the same number every time. This payout is unpredictable.
An interval depends on time. This payout depends on the number of plays.

questions.prompt: A child's screen time is taken away after they hit a sibling, and the hitting becomes less frequent. Which consequence is this?
hints: Ask whether something was added or removed, and whether the behaviour rose or fell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Something pleasant is removed (negative) and the behaviour decreases (punishment).

choices.label: Negative punishment
Positive punishment
Negative reinforcement
Positive reinforcement

questions.onCorrect: Something pleasant was removed and the behaviour fell: that is negative punishment.

misconceptions.feedback: Positive punishment adds something unpleasant. Here something pleasant was taken away.
Negative reinforcement makes the behaviour more likely. Here it became less frequent.
Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant and the behaviour rises. Here it fell.

questions.prompt: How many false positives are there?
hints: First find how many people do not have the disease.
Subtract the 1% who have it from 1,000.
Take 10% of that number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000 − 10 = 990 people do not have the disease; 10% of 990 = 99 false positives.

questions.onCorrect: False positives come only from people without the disease, a much bigger group than those who have it.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the error rate of the wrong group. False positives come from people who do not have the disease.
That takes the error rate of everyone. False positives come only from those who do not have the disease.

questions.prompt: What is the probability, as a percentage, that a person who tests positive has the disease? Give one decimal place.
hints: Restrict attention to people who tested positive.
The true positives are the people in that group who have the disease.
Divide 9 by the total number of positives and round.
questions.onCorrect: True positives over all positives, not the test's hit rate: most positives here are false alarms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the test's hit rate. The question asks how many positives are right.
That is the number of true positives. Turn it into a share of all positives.
That divides by the false positives alone. Divide by everyone flagged.

questions.prompt: What percentage of positive results are true positives?
hints: Count the people with and without the disease first.
Apply 90% to the first group and 10% to the second.
Divide true positives by all positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 have it and 90 test positive; 900 do not and 90 test positive; 90/180 = 50%.

questions.onCorrect: The same test, a different base rate: true positives now equal false positives, so a positive is a coin toss.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the hit rate. The question asks what share of positives are true.
That is the share who have the disease. Ask how many positives are true.

questions.prompt: 20% of a city's cabs are blue. A witness who names colours correctly 75% of the time says the cab was blue. What is the probability, as a percentage, that it was blue? Give one decimal place.
hints: Imagine 1,000 cabs: 200 blue and 800 green.
The witness calls 75% of blue cabs blue and 25% of green cabs blue.
Divide correct 'blue' calls by all 'blue' calls.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Per 1,000 cabs: 150 blue cabs called blue and 200 green cabs called blue; 150/350 = 42.9%.

questions.onCorrect: Count the cabs the witness calls blue: true calls over all calls. The many green cabs produce many wrong calls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the witness's accuracy, not the chance that this cab was blue.
That is the base rate alone. The witness's report adds evidence.
That is the share of 'blue' calls that were wrong.

questions.prompt: 2,000 people are tested for a condition that 5% have. The test detects 80% of cases and gives false positives for 10% of people without it. How many people test positive in total?
hints: 5% of 2,000 have the condition.
Find the true positives and the false positives separately.
Add the two groups of positives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 have it, 80 test positive; 1,900 do not, 190 test positive; 80 + 190 = 270.

questions.onCorrect: Add the true positives and the false positives: the flagged group is everyone with a positive result.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the true positives. Add the false positives too.
That counts only the false positives. Add the true positives too.

questions.prompt: A doctor judges a positive result from a 90%-accurate test as 90% likely to be right, ignoring that the disease is rare. What is this error called?
hints: The neglected number is how common the condition is to begin with.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Base-rate neglect: the prior frequency of the condition is ignored.

questions.onCorrect: Ignoring how rare a condition is when judging a result is base-rate neglect.

misconceptions.feedback: Confirmation bias favours evidence that fits what you believe. This error ignores how common the condition is.

questions.prompt: By how many percentage points did the medians differ?
hints: Compare the two median estimates, not the anchors.
The higher anchor produced the higher median.
Subtract the low-anchor median from the high-anchor median.
questions.onCorrect: Compare the two median estimates, not the anchors: an irrelevant number moved the typical guess.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the medians. The question asks how far apart the two medians are.
That is the gap between the anchors. Compare the medians.

questions.prompt: What is the anchoring index, (difference in medians) ÷ (difference in anchors)?
hints: Find the gap between the median estimates.
Find the gap between the anchors.
Divide the first gap by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The estimates moved a share of the way the anchors did: a clear pull, but not a full one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap in medians alone. Divide it by the gap between the anchors.
That divides the gap between anchors by the gap in medians. Invert it.

questions.prompt: In a sample of 600 English words containing k, 200 start with k and 400 have k as the third letter. What percentage start with k? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide words starting with k by all the k-words.
